questions.passageTitle: The repair that was never reported
questions.passage:
A. A fictional housing cooperative in Kaduna began publishing monthly maintenance figures after residents complained that broken fittings were taking too long to repair. Managers counted the jobs that appeared in a paper register and timed the interval between a report and its closure. On paper the service soon looked better. However, a resident on the third floor pointed out that nobody had yet repaired the loose handrail outside her flat. She had mentioned it informally to a caretaker, and the conversation had never become a recorded job.

B. The register presented a particular obstacle. Residents could fill it in only at the office, which closed before many commuters returned. The cooperative tried adding an evening reporting desk. It kept the procedure the same so it could see what happened when office hours alone changed. Within a month, reports of damaged entrance lights rose. The team treated this increase as evidence of previously unrecorded demand, because its inspection found no corresponding increase in broken lights.

C. Another difficulty became apparent when a supervisor followed several jobs from the register to the buildings. Some records marked as complete referred to a visit during which a technician had discovered that a spare part was needed. The technician’s visit was useful, but the resident still had the problem. To resolve this discrepancy the cooperative began distinguishing inspection, temporary action and completed repair. It also recorded whether a resident had confirmed that a fitting worked again.

D. The change made comparisons awkward. For several months the team published old and new measures side by side. The original series showed how promptly the office processed reports, whereas the new series indicated when residents could use the fittings again. Maintaining both gave the committee a bridge across the change in measurement. It could interpret past improvements without pretending that the two series measured the same thing.

E. Interviews revealed a separate cost that neither time series reflected. A resident could have a job completed within a week and still lose two afternoons waiting for an uncertain visit. The managers therefore tried letting residents choose between two shorter appointment windows. They monitored missed visits and invited residents to describe disruptions to work or care. The value of the service now depended in part on whether people could plan around it.

F. The committee eventually asked another cooperative to try the method. It suggested borrowing the distinction between an inspection and a completed repair, but leaving the choice of reporting channels and appointment hours to local residents. A building with a staffed entrance faced different constraints from one with a locked office. The committee’s aim was to share a way of recognising problems without prescribing a timetable for every building.
questions.prompt: Find the heading for paragraph A.
questions.explanation: The handrail case shows how a favourable set of figures could omit an unresolved problem.

questions.learningObjective: Locate a specific detail, example or comparison in a labelled paragraph.

questions.passageTitle: What a sound map leaves out
questions.passage:
A. A fictional field course asked students to map the sounds on a street beside a public park. A new footpath was planned, and the students wanted to know which stretches would suit conversation. Each pair carried a recorder and a notebook. They were told to make recordings from marked points rather than follow the sounds that attracted them. Without fixed positions, another group would have difficulty repeating the survey.

B. The first maps were drawn with a single colour scale. A darker patch meant the recorded signal was stronger. The scale was useful when comparing locations recorded with the same equipment, but the team noticed that a short burst from a gate could dominate a recording. The street might then look persistently loud even though the gate had struck only once. The students began adding a separate note for brief events.

C. A pair that worked near a playground made two recordings at the same mark, one while children were there and another after the group left. They heard distant traffic in both. In the first recording, voices were so prominent that the traffic was easy to overlook. The example showed why an audible source could seem to vanish when a second sound occupied the listener’s attention.

D. Some notes initially described the sounds as pleasant or unpleasant. The course leader asked pairs to record their impressions individually before talking to each other. One student found the sound of a football game reassuring, while another said it made the street hard to concentrate on. Their disagreement did not mean either had recorded the wrong location. It showed that an opinion about sound could depend on what a listener was trying to do.

E. One mark near the park wall was left blank on the published map. A loose cable had interrupted the recording there. The students could have coloured the spot to match the two closest marks, but a gap in the wall made it an unusual listening point. The published caption identified it as a location without usable evidence. A blank therefore meant missing data rather than silence.

F. The planning team eventually used the maps to select a few locations for further observations. Its members wanted to compare the same spots during school arrival, at midday and just before sunset. They also requested a trial conversation between two speakers standing an arm’s length apart. The trial would check whether the maps captured a difficulty that mattered to future users of the path.
questions.prompt: Which paragraph explains why researchers used marked positions?
questions.explanation: The marked positions allow other groups to repeat the survey at the same locations.

The scale was useful when comparing locations recorded with the same equipment, but the team noticed that a short burst from a gate could dominate a recording. The street might then look persistently loud even though the gate had struck only once. The students began adding a separate note for brief events.

C. A pair that worked near a playground made two recordings at the same mark, one while children were there and another after the group left. They heard distant traffic in both. In the first recording, voices were so prominent that the traffic was easy to overlook. The example showed why an audible source could seem to vanish when a second sound occupied the listener’s attention.

D. Some notes initially described the sounds as pleasant or unpleasant. The course leader asked pairs to record their impressions individually before talking to each other. One student found the sound of a football game reassuring, while another said it made the street hard to concentrate on. Their disagreement did not mean either had recorded the wrong location. It showed that an opinion about sound could depend on what a listener was trying to do.

E. One mark near the park wall was left blank on the published map. A loose cable had interrupted the recording there. The students could have coloured the spot to match the two closest marks, but a gap in the wall made it an unusual listening point. The published caption identified it as a location without usable evidence. A blank therefore meant missing data rather than silence.

F. The planning team eventually used the maps to select a few locations for further observations. Its members wanted to compare the same spots during school arrival, at midday and just before sunset. They also requested a trial conversation between two speakers standing an arm’s length apart. The trial would check whether the maps captured a difficulty that mattered to future users of the path.
questions.prompt: Identify the paragraph in which listeners respond differently to the same activity.
questions.explanation: The football game reassures one student and hinders concentration for another.

questions.passageTitle: Four designs for a seed exchange
questions.passage:
A. A fictional growers’ association in Benue planned to start an exchange for seeds saved from members’ own crops. It had storage space, a room for training and a small budget. The committee invited four members to suggest a way of organising the exchange. All wanted the project to support growers, but each saw a different risk in the first year.

B. Ada was concerned that packets with the same crop name might behave differently on different farms. She proposed that members grow small samples from several packets in marked rows on their own land. At the end of the season they would report when the plants flowered and how much shade the rows received. Reports would stay linked to the original packet. Ada argued that this would let newcomers see the conditions behind a promising result without declaring a single winner.

C. Musa focused on access for members who could spare neither the seed nor the time required to return it. He suggested lending a packet without requiring a replacement from the same crop. A grower could instead volunteer at an exchange day or help someone else record observations. He also proposed carrying a reserve over to the next year so one difficult harvest would not make the exchange dependent on new contributions.

D. Nneka expected interest in the exchange to be strong but saw a risk that a few popular packets would disappear before people from distant villages could arrive. She suggested collecting requests during a week and allocating scarce packets after the deadline. Where there were more applicants than packets, a draw would settle allocation. She wanted to publish the rules before accepting requests so members could judge the process without knowing who would benefit.

E. Sani was most concerned about what happened between seasons. He proposed using a packet label that stayed legible after repeated handling and keeping a second copy of its details outside the storage room. The second record would contain only enough information to trace the packet and its source. For Sani, a complicated form could make the label less reliable if members skipped fields or copied them inconsistently.

F. The association chose to try several proposals together. At a review meeting it planned to ask whether people could trace the origin of a sample, whether allocations had been understood, and whether members felt able to take part after a difficult season. It expected that performance on one of these measures might give little information about performance on another.
questions.prompt: Who proposes keeping records of growing conditions alongside performance?
questions.explanation: Ada asks for observations such as shade to remain linked to the original sample.
